definition: Behavior-based robotics (BBR) or behavioral robotics is an approach in robotics that focuses on robots that are able to exhibit complex-appearing behaviors despite little internal variable state to model its immediate environment, mostly gradually correcting its actions via sensory-motor links.
details: Behavior-based robotics (BBR) or behavioral robotics is an approach in robotics that focuses on robots that are able to exhibit complex-appearing behaviors despite little internal variable state to model its immediate environment, mostly gradually correcting its actions via sensory-motor links.

explainer.lead: Behavior-based robotics builds robots that act through direct, continually corrected links between what they sense and how they move. It matters because behavior that looks complicated can emerge without the robot maintaining a detailed internal model of its surroundings.

tiers.eli5: Imagine walking through a room with your eyes half closed: you notice what is nearby, take a step, and adjust as you go instead of memorizing a perfect map. A behavior-based robot works similarly, using simple sense-and-react rules again and again. Many small adjustments can make its movement look clever and complicated.
tiers.practitioner: An engineer implements this as closed-loop sensor-to-action behavior, with motor commands revised as new sensor readings arrive rather than through a detailed changing world model. The useful design focus is the combined behavior of sensing, action, and feedback, since every movement changes the next observation. Keeping little internal variable state does not remove the need to test whether repeated corrections produce stable, useful motion.
tiers.paperLevel: In plain-text notation, sensing produces s_t and the robot selects an action a_t through sensory-motor mappings, approximately a_t = f(s_t, z_t), where z_t represents little internal variable state. Action changes the robot's immediate sensory situation, producing s_(t+1), and repeated feedback gradually corrects its behavior. The defining target is complex-appearing behavior without relying on extensive internal state to model the immediate environment.

explainer.example: Suppose a small robot has a sensor that detects an obstacle close to its right side. Its sensory-motor response steers left, then the next reading guides another adjustment; when the obstacle is no longer close, it can continue forward. Repeating these local corrections can produce a complicated-looking route without maintaining a detailed map.
explainer.intuition: Instead of working out everything from a rich internal picture of the world, the robot keeps sensing and adjusting. Complexity appears in the ongoing interaction between the robot and its environment, not necessarily in a complicated internal representation.
howItWorks: Sensors capture information about the robot's immediate situation.
Sensory-motor links turn those readings into actions.
The actions change the robot's position or interaction with its environment.
New sensor readings feed back into further adjustments.
Repeating this loop can produce complex-appearing behavior with little internal variable state.
explainer.whyItMatters: It shows that useful, complex-appearing robot behavior can arise from ongoing sensory feedback rather than extensive internal environmental state. This makes the robot's interaction with its immediate environment central to explaining what it does.
misconceptions: Little internal variable state does not mean absolutely no internal state.
Complex-appearing behavior does not require a detailed internal map.
The approach is not a single unchanging reaction: actions are gradually corrected through continuing sensory feedback.
